name: Deuteronomy

objectives.text: Identify Moses as the leader who spoke God's words to Israel just before they entered the promised land
Recite the command to love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul, and might
Retell how God told Israel's parents to talk about his words at home, on the road, at bedtime, and in the morning
Identify Joshua as the leader God chose to bring Israel into the land after Moses
Explain what the Shema teaches about God being the one and only LORD
Explain why Moses repeated the Ten Commandments to a new generation and how this connects to the name Deuteronomy, meaning second law
Explain from Deuteronomy that God chose Israel because of his own love and promise and not because of their size or righteousness
Compare the covenant blessings promised for obedience with the curses warned for disobedience
Describe the laws in Deuteronomy that protect widows, orphans, sojourners, and the poor and explain how they reflect God's own character
Explain how Jesus answered each of Satan's temptations by quoting Deuteronomy
Outline Deuteronomy as a series of speeches by Moses using the headings that open each section
Explain the call to choose life in its setting of covenant renewal on the plains of Moab
Explain why Moses died on Mount Nebo outside the land and what the closing epitaph says about his unique role
Analyze the law of the king and use it to evaluate Solomon's reign
Explain the promise of a prophet like Moses and how the New Testament identifies its fulfillment in Christ
Explain the command to worship at the place the LORD will choose and trace how it points to the temple and to Jesus' teaching on true worship
Analyze the Song of Moses as a witness that rehearses God's faithfulness and Israel's coming unfaithfulness
Analyze how Deuteronomy follows the pattern of ancient Near Eastern suzerain-vassal treaties and what that pattern shows about God's covenant with Israel
Trace the theme of the heart in Deuteronomy from the command to circumcise one's heart to the promise that God himself will do it
Analyze how Deuteronomy's warnings of exile and promises of return anticipate the later history of Israel
Explain how the Reformed tradition uses Deuteronomy's commands not to add to or take from God's word to support the sufficiency of Scripture
Evaluate the Deuteronomistic History hypothesis and critical dating theories against the book's own claims about Moses writing the law
Compose an essay tracing how the Prophets, Jesus, and Paul draw on Deuteronomy and arguing for its place in the theology of the whole canon

changes: Kept and sharpened the real competencies: Moses' final speeches, the love command, the Shema, teaching children, the second-law name, blessings and curses, the king law, Jesus' temptation, Moses' death, the treaty structure, the heart theme, the Deuteronomistic History hypothesis, and the canonical essay. The Shema now teaches the oneness of God. The heart theme is now a trace from command to promise. The essay is tied to specific uses of Deuteronomy in later Scripture. Dropped two items. 'Observe that God wants us to remember His laws' was vague and overlapped other objectives. 'Defend the unity of the Law' was an unclear competency that belongs with the Law and Gospel sibling. Rewrote 'obedience brings blessings' as a confessionally anchored comparison. Recast 'Apply the command to teach children' as a retelling of the text. Added Joshua's succession, election by grace, care for the vulnerable, the call to choose life in covenant renewal, the prophet like Moses, the central sanctuary, the Song of Moses, exile and return, and the use of Deuteronomy for the sufficiency of Scripture. Replaced the whole-section references with verse ranges. Added catechism and confession anchors only where they state the doctrine taught.
